newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss back government probe of Nazi-era banking.
newsitem.headline: Swiss back government probe of Nazi-era banking.

text.p: The Swiss government, under pressure to explain the fate of Nazi gold, on Monday endorsed an official inquiry into the whereabouts of both Nazi and Jewish wealth held by secretive Swiss banks during World War Two.
The cabinet, of Federal Council, gave its backing to a bill in the works since May that would create a commission of experts empowered to lift Swiss bank secrecy laws.
Parliament must give final approval to the bill for a commission of historians and financial experts.
"The investigation will cover the lost or stolen assets of victims of National Socialism (Nazism) as well as Nazi assets brought into Switzerland," a cabinet statement said.

At the same time, Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti and Swiss National Bank president Hans Meyer called a news conference later on Monday to present the inquiry plan and react to allegations Switzerland may still be harbouring Nazi gold.

"The series of international media stories in the past week about the issue of Nazi gold has created a lot of questions, and we want the responsible people to be available to answer these questions," Cotti's spokesman said.

Berne politicians said the government was fighting to protect Switzerland's international reputation -- and its role as a world financial centre -- by actively seeking to uncover the banking secrets of the war years.

The bill creating an historical commission has already passed parliament's legal affairs committee, an indication that it should be supported by both chambers in the autumn session that opened on Monday.
Under Switzerland's system of direct democracy, a referendum can be called on the bill if at least 50,000 voters sign a petition. But a referendum is not required.
Swiss leaders have been under pressure to counter speculation that Nazi gold was still hidden in the neutral country since a British Foreign Office report last week.

The report, although based on documents long since public and known by historians, revived allegations that the Swiss kept nearly nine-tenths of gold bought from Hitler's Germany rather than hand it over to the Allies after World war Two.

International headlines about Nazi gold added to pressure on the government to clear up the fate of money and treasures deposited in Swiss banks by both Nazis and their victims before and during World War Two.

Swiss politicians have been working on the historical inquiry bill since May, after world Jewish groups wrung an agreement from Swiss banks to search for accounts that may have been left by victims of the Holocaust.
Politicians were prompted by fears that the slowness of Swiss banks to open their Nazi-era records was damaging Switzerland's reputation.

They were also moved by international criticism that the Swiss government only got around last year, 50 years after World War Two ended, to apologising for turning back German Jewish refugees from 1938 to 1945 to face death in Nazi camps.
